questions.prompt: The inverse BFGS update produces a matrix \(W_+\) that satisfies
options: \(W_+ y = s\), the secant equation written for an inverse approximation
questions.explanation: If \(B\) approximates the Hessian and \(B s = y\), an inverse approximation should send \(y\) back to \(s\). The BFGS formula is built so that this holds. The zero matrix sends \(y\) to zero, not to \(s\). Sending every step \(s\) to zero is the opposite equation. The formula divides by \(y^T s\), so it needs that product to be nonzero, and the positive-definite case needs it positive.

questions.prompt: Start from the identity. Take \(s = (1,\ 0)\) and \(y = (2,\ 0)\). What is the \((1,1)\) entry of the inverse BFGS update?
questions.explanation: Here \(y^T s = 2\) and \(\rho = 1/2\). The matrix \(I - \rho s y^T\) equals \(\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Adding \(\rho s s^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) produces \(\begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). The \((1,1)\) entry is \(1/2\). The secant check: this matrix times \(y\) equals \(s\). Reporting \(2\) is \(y^T s\). Reporting \(1\) is the untouched \((2,2)\) entry. Reporting \(-1/2\) flips the sign of the rank-one term.

questions.prompt: If the current inverse approximation is positive definite, the BFGS update stays positive definite when
questions.explanation: The update divides by \(y^T s\). When that product is positive and the old approximation is positive definite, the new one is positive definite. A zero product makes the formula undefined. A negative product can introduce a negative eigenvalue. A zero step has \(y^T s = 0\) as well, so there is nothing to update from.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of one BFGS iteration in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The line search needs a direction, and the direction is the inverse approximation times the negative gradient. The displacement and the gradient change are measured on the step that was accepted, so they come after the line search. The reciprocal \(\rho\) divides by \(y^T s\), which uses the pair just formed. The formula names \(\rho\), \(s\), and \(y\), so it comes last. Forming \(y\) before the step is taken would compare gradients at the wrong points.

steps: Apply the current inverse approximation to the negative gradient to get a direction.
Accept a step length along that direction that satisfies the Wolfe conditions.
Form the displacement \(s\) and the gradient change \(y\) from that accepted step.
Set \(\rho\) to the reciprocal of \(y^T s\).
Replace the inverse approximation by the BFGS formula that uses \(\rho\), \(s\), \(y\), and the previous approximation.

questions.prompt: In one variable the inverse BFGS update depends only on the step \(s\) and the gradient change \(y\). The new inverse approximation equals
questions.explanation: The secant equation for an inverse approximation says the new value times \(y\) equals \(s\). There is only one such number, \(s/y\). The old approximation cancels: the factor in front of it is \(1 - s y / (y s) = 0\). Both declared names appear. The ratio \(y/s\) is the Hessian approximation, not its inverse. The product \(s y\) is not dimensionless in the same way and does not send \(y\) to \(s\). The sum \(s + y\) fails the secant equation whenever \(y \ne 1\).

questions.prompt: The current inverse approximation is positive definite. Which pairs have \(y^T s > 0\), so the BFGS update is defined and stays positive definite?
questions.explanation:
The test is the sign of the inner product. The formula is undefined at zero and can lose positive definiteness when the product is negative.
• \((1)(2) + (0)(0) = 2 > 0\).
• \((1)(-1) = -1 < 0\).
• \((1)(1) + (1)(2) = 3 > 0\).
• \((1)(0) + (0)(1) = 0\), so \(\rho\) is undefined.
• \((2)(0) + (-1)(-2) = 2 > 0\).

questions.prompt: A note runs inverse BFGS from the identity with \(s = (1,\ 0)\) and \(y = (-1,\ 0)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The product is \(( -1)(1) = -1\). With \(\rho = -1\), the rank-one term \(\rho s s^T\) contributes \(-1\) in the \((1,1)\) entry, and the conjugate term contributes nothing there, so the entry is \(-1\). The matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), whose eigenvalues are \(-1\) and \(1\). Positive definiteness needs every eigenvalue positive, and the BFGS argument requires \(y^T s > 0\). This pair fails that hypothesis, so the formula does not preserve positive definiteness.

steps: That diagonal result has a negative eigenvalue.
The updated matrix is positive definite for every \(y\) and \(s\).
reasons: Positive definiteness of the update needs \(y^T s > 0\). Here the product is \(-1\), and the \((1,1)\) entry is negative.
The \((1,1)\) entry of the update is not \(-1\).

questions.prompt: Start from the identity. Take \(s = (1,\ 0)\) and \(y = (4,\ 0)\). What is the \((1,1)\) entry of the inverse BFGS update?
questions.explanation: Here \(y^T s = 4\) and \(\rho = 1/4\). Then \(\rho s s^T\) has \((1,1)\) entry \(1/4\), and \(I - \rho s y^T\) has a zero in that entry. The updated \((1,1)\) entry is \(1/4\). The secant check: \((1/4) \cdot 4 = 1\), which is the first component of \(s\). Reporting \(4\) is \(y^T s\). Reporting \(1\) would be the entry from a pair with \(y = s\). Reporting \(1/2\) is the entry for \(y = (2,\ 0)\), a different gradient change.

questions.prompt: Locally, successive error ratios of BFGS tend to \(0\). That rate is
options: sublinear, because the ratios go to \(0\)
the same squared-error bound that Newton's method has, with a universal constant
questions.explanation: Superlinear convergence means the error goes to zero and the ratio of successive errors goes to zero. That is the local claim for BFGS. It is faster than a linear rate, whose ratio tends to a positive constant, and it is weaker than a quadratic bound, which Newton's method has under a Lipschitz Hessian. Tendencies of the ratio toward zero are not divergence. Sublinear convergence is the opposite pattern: the error goes to zero while the successive ratio tends to \(1\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A different Hessian-free method builds conjugate directions from gradients and finishes a positive definite quadratic in at most \(n\) steps. That method is
options: a BFGS update that stores a dense inverse approximation on every quadratic
a Newton step with the exact Hessian
a line search with no direction
questions.explanation: Conjugate gradients generate the next direction from the latest gradient and the previous direction. On a positive definite quadratic with exact line searches it reaches the minimizer in at most \(n\) steps, and it does not store an \(n \times n\) inverse Hessian. BFGS does store that approximation. A Newton step with the exact Hessian is not Hessian-free. A line search needs a direction.

questions.prompt: An inverse approximation is diagonal with entries \(1/2\) and \(1\), and the gradient is \((2,\ 0)\). The search direction is minus that approximation times the gradient. What is the first component of the direction?
questions.explanation: The first component of the approximation times the gradient is \((1/2) \cdot 2 = 1\). The search direction flips the sign, so the first component is \(-1\). The second component is \(0\). Reporting \(1\) forgets the minus sign in front of the approximation. Reporting \(-2\) multiplies by the gradient and skips the \(1/2\). Reporting \(1/2\) is the diagonal entry, not the direction.

questions.prompt: A positive definite inverse approximation \(W\) makes \(d = -W \nabla f\) a descent direction. Using such a \(W\) as the metric of a projected step is the idea of
options: a simplex ratio test with no metric
a power iteration on a skew-symmetric matrix
a line search that ignores the direction
questions.explanation: The direction \(-W g\) has directional derivative \(-g^T W g\), which is negative when \(W\) is positive definite and \(g \ne 0\). A projected method can take that step in the \(W\)-metric and then project. BFGS is one way to keep a positive definite \(W\). A simplex ratio test uses the signs of tableau entries. A skew-symmetric matrix does not give a positive \(g^T W g\). A line search does not replace the metric.
